title: Eco-friendly, economical driving
summary: Driving that saves fuel, wears the vehicle less, and harms the environment less — and is also safer.

lessons.title: Smooth driving: less fuel, less wear
lessons.summary: Looking well ahead, gentle acceleration and coasting correctly save fuel without giving up anything.
lessons.body:
The driving that saves the most fuel is not slow driving — it is **smooth** driving: fewer hard brakes, fewer sudden bursts of acceleration, more looking ahead.

# Looking far ahead, driving smoothly
A driver who looks far ahead of the vehicle spots early a light about to change, a jam forming, or a vehicle slowing down — and can ease off the accelerator gradually instead of braking hard at the last moment. A larger gap from the vehicle in front gives you exactly that time: see [[lesson:sd-following|Keeping a safe distance from the vehicle in front]]. This also has a direct safety benefit: fewer emergency stops mean fewer rear-end collisions — detail in the [[chapter:defensive-driving|Safe driving and defensive driving]] chapter.

# Gentle acceleration and early gear changes
Hard acceleration burns fuel much faster than gentle acceleration, and usually does not significantly shorten your arrival time in urban driving — especially when it ends at a red light. In a manual vehicle, shifting to a higher gear as early as possible — without labouring the engine — saves fuel; in an automatic vehicle, "Eco" mode does this for the driver. A sharp turn or entering a bend too fast also wears the tyres and forces extra acceleration afterwards — a smooth turn saves both fuel and rubber.

# Coasting correctly
When approaching a red light, a Stop sign or a traffic jam, you can ease off the accelerator early and let the vehicle slow down by itself while coasting — without braking too early and without accelerating until the last moment. Important: this kind of coasting is done **in gear**, not in neutral. Shifting to neutral while driving reduces control and does not meaningfully save fuel — for why this is especially dangerous on descents, see the [[chapter:drivetrain|Powertrain]] chapter.

# Cruise control on the open road
On a long drive on the open road, [[term:cruise-control|cruise control]] keeps a steady speed without unnecessary acceleration and braking — it usually saves fuel compared with driving where your foot keeps moving between the accelerator and the brake. It is less suited to heavy traffic, rain, or a road with climbs and descents that need a quick response.

:::tip
Aerodynamic drag works against you more and more as speed rises: air resistance grows roughly with the square of the speed, so driving at a steady, moderate speed on the open road uses less fuel per kilometre than driving faster with the same braking further on.
:::

# Matching your speed to the flow, not "cutting" lanes
Switching lanes often to "gain" a few places in a jam almost never shortens your arrival time, and forces repeated braking and accelerating that burns extra fuel. A driver who matches their speed to the flow of traffic, keeps to a lane and plans turns ahead of time arrives at roughly the same time — with less fuel, less wear, and lower risk.
keyPoints: Looking far ahead and keeping a large gap from the vehicle in front let you slow down gradually instead of braking hard — and are also safer.
Gentle acceleration and shifting to a higher gear early save fuel; a smooth turn saves both fuel and tyres.
Correct coasting = easing off the accelerator early, in gear, not shifting to neutral while driving.
Cruise control saves fuel on the open road, but is less suited to heavy traffic or changing conditions.
Switching lanes often to get ahead in a jam almost never saves time, and costs extra fuel.

lessons.title: Your vehicle: maintenance that saves fuel
lessons.summary: Tyre pressure, unnecessary load and unnecessary idling — all of them make every drive more expensive.
lessons.body:
It is not only your driving style that decides how much fuel the vehicle burns — the condition of the vehicle itself matters too.

# Tyre pressure
[[term:tyre-pressure|Tyre pressure]] lower than recommended increases rolling resistance, and therefore also [[term:fuel-economy|fuel consumption]] — and shortens the tyre's life. Check the pressure cold (before a long drive) at least once a month, to the value set by the manufacturer, not by feel or by how the tyre looks. Full detail on tyre types and checking them is in the [[chapter:tyres|Tyres and wheels]] chapter.

# Load and roof racks
Extra weight in the vehicle, and especially additions that disturb airflow such as a roof box or a bike rack, increase fuel consumption — the box mainly at higher speed, where air resistance dominates. Remove roof equipment you are not using, and do not drive around with unnecessary items in the boot "just in case". The number of passengers in a private car has almost no effect on consumption — the difference between driving with one passenger and with four is negligible compared with a roof box or underinflated tyres.

# Air conditioning and windows
Air conditioning increases fuel consumption, especially in slow urban driving. Using the recirculation setting instead of drawing in outside air reduces the load on the air conditioner most of the time, and cools the cabin faster. At high speed on the open road, open windows increase air resistance more than the air conditioner would cost — a general rule of thumb, not an exact law of physics in every vehicle.

# Unnecessary idling
Running the engine while stationary without driving burns fuel for no benefit and adds local pollution, in exactly the place where people are standing or sitting near you. The law explicitly forbids this for buses: you must not start or run the engine of a parked bus until passengers are boarding, except to build up air in its pneumatic system — and it may be run for up to {{fact:eco.bus_idle_before_boarding_max_min}} in advance before boarding (regulation 72A). The idea applies to every vehicle: during a long wait — beside a school, in a parking spot before you go into a building, or in a jam that has come to a complete stop — it is better to turn off the engine than to leave it idling.

# Routine maintenance
A clogged air filter, worn spark plugs or old oil make it harder for the engine to work efficiently and increase fuel consumption — alongside the risk of a breakdown. Cheap, non-original replacement parts may fit less well and also harm efficiency. Even a "check engine" light left ignored can hide a fault that significantly increases fuel consumption, before it turns into a more expensive fault — detail on warning lights is in the [[chapter:dashboard|Dashboard and warning lights]] chapter. More on routine maintenance, choosing a garage and the exhaust system is in the [[chapter:maintenance|Routine maintenance and the annual test]] and [[chapter:engine|The engine and its systems]] chapters.
keyPoints: Low tyre pressure increases fuel consumption and shortens tyre life — check cold, to the manufacturer's recommendation.
Extra weight and a roof box increase fuel consumption; remove roof equipment you are not using.
Recirculating air eases the load on the air conditioner; on a fast road, open windows increase air resistance more than the air conditioner would.
Unnecessary idling burns fuel for no benefit; a parked bus must not run its engine before boarding beyond {{fact:eco.bus_idle_before_boarding_max_min}} (reg. 72A).
Routine maintenance — filters, spark plugs, oil, genuine parts — directly affects fuel consumption.

lessons.title: Planning your trip: less fuel, less stress
lessons.summary: A planned trip saves both time and fuel — and sometimes there is no need to drive at all.
lessons.body:
Before you shut the door and start the engine, a few simple decisions already decide how much the trip will cost in fuel.

# Plan before you set out
A cold engine uses more fuel per kilometre in the first few minutes of a drive, so combining several errands into one trip saves more than several separate short trips, each starting from a cold engine. Planning a route in advance also avoids unnecessary trips caused by a wrong turn, and sometimes a slightly longer route on a fast, flowing road uses less fuel than a shorter route full of stops. Many navigation apps now also offer an "economical" route option, which favours a continuous flow over the shortest possible distance. Warming up the engine while idling before you set off does not make the trip more efficient — a modern engine actually warms up faster while driving gently in the first few minutes.

# Peak hours
In a jam you drive in constant stop-and-start — every acceleration after a stop burns fuel, so fuel consumption per kilometre in a jam is significantly higher than in flowing traffic over the same distance. When you can be flexible about your departure time, driving outside peak hours saves fuel, time and stress alike — and also reduces the risk of stop-and-start accidents, among the most common accidents in heavy traffic.

# Carpooling and public transport
Sharing a ride between several people in one vehicle, or switching to public transport when it is available and practical, reduces the total amount of fuel burned per person and the load on the road — and also lowers the cost of the trip for each passenger. A bus or a light rail train carrying dozens of passengers in one trip uses far less energy per passenger than a private car with one occupant, even taking into account that they also run when not full. For the rules on public-transport lanes, which sometimes also allow a vehicle with several occupants to use them, see [[lesson:sr-transit|Public-transport lanes, stops and taxis]].

# Electric vehicles — a bit different
In an electric vehicle, "fuel consumption" is measured in kWh per hundred kilometres instead of litres per hundred kilometres, and much of the saving comes from regenerative braking, which returns energy to the battery instead of wasting it as heat in the brakes. The principles of smooth driving still apply, but trip planning gains another layer: on a long drive, it is worth planning charging stops in advance instead of finding yourself with a low range far from a charging point. Extreme temperatures, heating and air conditioning reduce the real-world range more than in a vehicle with a combustion engine, so it is worth building in a larger safety margin when planning a long route in winter or in a heatwave. The full differences between an electric vehicle and one with a combustion engine are detailed in the [[chapter:ev-hybrid|Electric and hybrid vehicles]] chapter.
keyPoints: Combining errands into one trip saves more than a cold engine started again and again.
Driving in a jam burns more fuel per kilometre than flowing driving; avoid peak hours when you can.
Carpooling and public transport reduce the total amount of fuel burned, the load on the roads, and the cost per passenger.
In an electric vehicle, efficiency is measured in kWh, regenerative braking returns energy to the battery, and on a long drive you plan charging stops in advance.

lessons.title: Emissions, noise and the environment
lessons.summary: A vehicle that drives economically also pollutes less and is quieter — and that is also a legal requirement.
lessons.body:
Saving fuel and polluting less are two sides of the same coin: an engine that works efficiently burns less fuel and emits less. The earlier lessons in this chapter showed how to achieve that in practice — here you see why it is also a requirement of the law, not just an economic choice.

# The law forbids excess pollution and noise
:::law
You must not drive a vehicle, and must not leave it standing on the road, if it emits gases, smoke, oil or fuel beyond what is normal for a vehicle of its kind, or to an extent that may bother road users or endanger safety (regulation 155). Likewise, you must not drive a vehicle that makes excessive noise as a result of a fault, neglected maintenance, or a badly arranged load — and on an urban road you must not cause more noise than is needed for the vehicle to run properly (regulation 157).
:::

# What causes unnecessary pollution
A clogged air filter, a badly calibrated injection system, or a problem in the exhaust system all increase both pollution and fuel consumption. Blue smoke from the exhaust suggests burning oil, black smoke suggests an overly rich fuel-air mixture — in both cases the engine pollutes more and uses more fuel per kilometre. Detail on the exhaust system, the catalytic converter and the particulate filter is in the [[chapter:engine|The engine and its systems]] chapter. The annual test also checks emissions, alongside the vehicle's other systems — detail in the [[chapter:maintenance|Routine maintenance and the annual test]] chapter.

# Noise is not just a nuisance
Sounding the horn without real need, or accelerating hard and noisily in a residential neighbourhood at night, disturbs the surroundings — and can also be an offence: {{fine:horn-misuse}} for misusing the horn. Smooth driving, as covered in [[lesson:eco-smooth|Smooth driving: less fuel, less wear]], is also quieter, wears the vehicle less and saves fuel — all the benefits together.

# It is also a safety matter
Thick smoke coming from a vehicle blocks the view of drivers behind it, and a quieter engine helps the driver themselves hear horns, sirens and traffic around them — not just save fuel. In stationary traffic in a tunnel or a long jam between tall buildings, accumulated emissions also affect people sitting in a vehicle with the windows closed, not only pedestrians and the outside environment.

# What all the earlier lessons connect to
A well-maintained vehicle, driven smoothly and planned ahead as covered in the three previous lessons, harms the environment less, costs less, and is usually also safer. Saving fuel, reducing pollution and safety are not three separate goals competing with each other — they are the result of the same correct driving.
keyPoints: You must not drive a vehicle that emits excess pollution (reg. 155) or makes excessive noise (reg. 157).
Routine maintenance of filters and the injection system reduces both pollution and fuel consumption; the annual test also checks emissions.
Misusing the horn is an offence in its own right: {{fine:horn-misuse}}.
Smooth, quiet driving also helps the driver hear and notice their surroundings — alongside the fuel saving.
